subject: physics
chapter_title: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits

concepts.title: Energy Band Theory and Classification of Solids
concepts.definition: Solids are differentiated into conductors, semiconductors, and insulators based on the magnitude of the forbidden energy gap separating the valence and conduction bands.
concepts.key_idea: Large gap produces an insulator, small gap yields a semiconductor, and zero gap or overlap creates a metal.
question_patterns: distinguish between metals, semiconductors and insulators on the basis of energy band theory
why does diamond behave as an insulator while silicon behaves as a semiconductor
compare the energy band gap of carbon, silicon and germanium
explain the difference in electrical conductivity between metals and semiconductors using band structure
what is the magnitude of the forbidden band gap in an insulator compared to a semiconductor

solution_steps.action: identify the valence band and conduction band levels
solution_steps.explain: The highest filled band at 0 K is the valence band (Ev) and the lowest unfilled band is the conduction band (Ec).
For metals Eg is approximately 0 eV; for semiconductors Eg is less than 3 eV; for insulators Eg exceeds 3 eV.

concepts.title: Total Current in an Intrinsic Semiconductor
concepts.definition: In an undoped semiconductor, thermal excitation generates identical numbers of free electrons and holes, both of which migrate under an electric field to contribute to the net current.
concepts.key_idea: The total electrical current equals the sum of the electron drift current and the hole drift current.
question_patterns: find the total current in a semiconductor given electron and hole currents
calculate the net current when electron current is ... and hole current is ...
what is the total current flowing through an intrinsic semiconductor crystal
determine the combined current from electron and hole drift components
compute the total crystal current when both carrier types move under an electric field

solution_steps.action: add electron current and hole current
solution_steps.explain: Both carriers move in opposite directions under an applied field and thus their conventional currents add together.

concepts.title: Carrier Concentration and Mass Action Law in Extrinsic Semiconductors
concepts.definition: Under thermal equilibrium in any semiconductor, the product of the electron concentration and the hole concentration remains constant and equal to the square of the intrinsic concentration.
concepts.key_idea: Doping vastly increases one carrier density while suppressing the other such that their product remains fixed at ni squared.
question_patterns: calculate the minority carrier concentration in a doped semiconductor
find the hole concentration in an n-type silicon crystal doped with donor atoms
determine the electron concentration in a p-type semiconductor
given the intrinsic carrier concentration and majority carrier density, compute the minority carrier density
what is the concentration of holes when silicon with intrinsic density ... is doped with ... donor atoms

solution_steps.explain: The product of equilibrium electron and hole concentrations is equal to ni squared.

solution_steps.action: divide squared intrinsic concentration by the majority carrier concentration
solution_steps.explain: Use the mass action law to obtain the minority carrier concentration.

concepts.title: Extrinsic Doping and Semiconductor Classification
concepts.definition: Doping tetravalent crystals with pentavalent donor impurities yields n-type semiconductors, whereas doping with trivalent acceptor impurities creates p-type semiconductors while keeping overall crystal neutrality.
concepts.formula: n_type: ne >> nh; p_type: nh >> ne
concepts.key_idea: Donor impurities provide majority electrons, acceptor impurities supply majority holes, and total crystal charge remains strictly zero.
question_patterns: identify whether a crystal is n-type or p-type when doped with phosphorus or boron
explain why a doped semiconductor remains electrically neutral despite having excess free carriers
why do pentavalent dopants act as donors while trivalent dopants act as acceptors
distinguish between majority and minority carriers in n-type and p-type silicon
verify the electrical neutrality condition of an extrinsic semiconductor

solution_steps.action: identify dopant valency and nature of impurity
solution_steps.explain: Pentavalent elements (P, As, Sb) provide free conduction electrons (donors); trivalent elements (B, Al, In) provide vacancies/holes (acceptors).
The total positive charge of uncompensated donor ions and holes equals the total negative charge of electrons and acceptor ions.

concepts.title: p-n Junction Formation and Barrier Potential
concepts.definition: A p-n junction establishes a space-charge depletion region devoid of mobile carriers through diffusion, which sets up an internal electric field that drives an opposing drift current until equilibrium is attained.
concepts.key_idea: Carrier concentration gradients drive diffusion until the built-in barrier potential creates a matching drift current, resulting in zero net current at equilibrium.
question_patterns: explain how a depletion region is formed in an unbiased p-n junction
why cannot a p-n junction be created by physically pressing a p-type slab against an n-type slab
describe the role of diffusion current and drift current in reaching junction equilibrium
what gives rise to the barrier potential across a semiconductor diode junction
how does the width of the depletion layer affect the built-in electric field at equilibrium

solution_steps.action: describe diffusion of majority carriers across the interface
solution_steps.explain: Electrons diffuse from the n-side to the p-side and holes diffuse from the p-side to the n-side, leaving uncompensated immobile ion cores.

solution_steps.action: describe the establishment of the space-charge region and opposing drift
solution_steps.explain: The positive ions on the n-side and negative ions on the p-side establish an electric field from n to p that causes minority carrier drift until net current is zero.

concepts.title: Dynamic Resistance of a Junction Diode
concepts.definition: The dynamic or ac resistance of a p-n junction diode is defined as the ratio of an incremental change in the applied bias voltage to the corresponding incremental change in the resulting diode current.
concepts.key_idea: Dynamic resistance represents the reciprocal slope of the diode V-I characteristic curve at a given operating point.
question_patterns: calculate the dynamic resistance of a diode given change in voltage and change in current
find the ac resistance of a p-n junction when voltage changes by ... and current changes by ...
what is the forward dynamic resistance of a silicon diode operating between ... and ...
determine the dynamic resistance from the slope of the forward V-I characteristic
compute the dynamic resistance of a reverse biased junction diode

solution_steps.action: divide the incremental voltage by the incremental current
solution_steps.explain: Dynamic resistance is the ratio of delta_v to delta_i.

concepts.title: Diode Biasing: Forward and Reverse Characteristics
concepts.definition: Forward bias reduces the potential barrier and narrows the depletion width leading to large diffusion current, whereas reverse bias widens the barrier resulting in only a minute drift-driven saturation current.
concepts.formula: V_net_forward = V0 - V; V_net_reverse = V0 + V
concepts.key_idea: A diode conducts heavily in forward bias once beyond the knee voltage and behaves as a near open circuit in reverse bias up to breakdown.
question_patterns: explain the behavior of a p-n junction diode under forward bias and reverse bias
why does the depletion layer width decrease during forward bias and increase during reverse bias
what is meant by threshold voltage or cut-in voltage of a diode
describe the variation of current with voltage in the forward and reverse bias of a silicon diode
explain reverse saturation current and breakdown voltage in a semiconductor diode

solution_steps.explain: Connecting p to positive and n to negative lowers the barrier height to (V0 - V), enabling minority carrier injection and milliampere-scale forward current.
Connecting p to negative and n to positive elevates the barrier height to (V0 + V), reducing diffusion current to zero and permitting only a tiny microampere drift current.

concepts.title: Full-Wave and Half-Wave Rectification Ripple Frequency
concepts.definition: A rectifier converts alternating voltage into unidirectional pulsating voltage: a half-wave rectifier outputs pulses at the input line frequency, while a full-wave rectifier delivers pulses at twice the input line frequency.
concepts.key_idea: A full-wave rectifier conducts during both half-cycles of the alternating input, thereby doubling the output ripple frequency.
question_patterns: find the output ripple frequency of a full-wave rectifier given the input ac frequency
calculate the output frequency of a full-wave rectifier when the mains frequency is ...
what is the output frequency for a full-wave rectifier operating at an input frequency of ...
determine the ripple frequency across the load of a full-wave rectifier circuit
compute the output pulsating frequency of a center-tap full-wave rectifier

solution_steps.action: multiply the input ac supply frequency by 2
solution_steps.explain: Because both halves of the input sine wave appear in the rectified output, the output period is halved and frequency is doubled.
